messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rosario is a 61-year-old Salvadoran-American woman who has driven city buses for nearly two decades. She is married, lives with her husband in a modest home in a mid-sized city, and until eighteen months ago was regarded by her dispatcher as one of the most dependable drivers on the route. That changed on a Tuesday morning in early winter when, stopped at a red light with a full bus, she watched a sedan run the intersection at speed and strike a pedestrian — a young man who had just stepped off her bus seconds earlier. The impact was immediate and catastrophic. Rosario saw the collision through her windshield at close range: the sound, the arc of the body, the blood spreading across the asphalt. She could not leave her passengers to go to him. By the time paramedics arrived, he was dead. She has not been able to stop asking herself why she did not call out to him, why she did not hold the doors a moment longer, why she simply sat there while he died in the street.

In the months that followed, the memory refused to recede. It does not arrive as a narrative she can observe from a distance — when it comes, Rosario is back at that intersection, the windshield in front of her, the sound filling her ears, the cold air on her hands on the wheel. She describes it as completely real across every sense at once: the smell of the diesel exhaust, the particular grey of the winter morning, the helplessness that floods her chest before she can name it as a feeling. At other times there is no image at all, only a sudden wave of grief and terror so intense she must grip a surface to stay upright, the emotional weight of the event arriving without any picture to explain it. Because the memory carries no clear sense of pastness — it feels, as she puts it, like it is still happening — Rosario has come to believe that she is not a person who survived something terrible, but a person who is still inside it.

That belief has shaped everything. She has come to see herself as someone who failed catastrophically: she should have protected that young man, and she did not. She is certain she will never forgive herself. On her worst days she is not sure her life holds enough worth to continue, a thought she has not shared with her husband but which sits with her in the early hours of the morning. These appraisals, once established, have made the memory more accessible rather than less — each time she condemns herself, the scene reasserts itself with fresh intensity, as though her guilt keeps the intersection perpetually lit.

The triggers she encounters on her route are now unbearable. The sight of blood — even a minor injury on a passenger — pulls her instantly back to the asphalt and the spreading red. A near-miss in traffic, any moment in which she feels she cannot control what is about to happen, or the flash of cars converging at an intersection, collapses the distance between then and now. Because the triggers reliably return her to the memory, and the memory reliably returns her to the conviction that she is guilty and irreparably damaged, Rosario has developed a set of private rituals she performs before and during each shift: counting in a particular sequence, touching the wheel in a fixed pattern, repeating a phrase under her breath — all aimed at preventing another catastrophe. She understands, dimly, that these rituals do nothing, but their absence feels like an invitation to disaster. She also avoids any form of physical contact with others, including her husband's hand on her shoulder, because touch now feels like an intrusion into a body she no longer fully trusts. She has quietly removed photographs of the young man from news coverage and avoids the street where he was buried. These strategies bring momentary relief but sustain the architecture of her distress — each ritual performed confirms that danger is real and imminent, each piece of grief avoided keeps the loss unprocessed, and each act of avoidance returns her, sooner or later, to the image she is trying to escape.

Over the past year Rosario has taken four medical leaves, her route coverage has become unreliable, and her supervisor has gently but formally noted her performance. Her husband knows something is deeply wrong but does not know what to do with her silence. What finally brought her to seek help was a shift last month in which a minor fender-bender two cars ahead of her on the route triggered a full reliving episode while she had passengers on board. She pulled over, shaking, and sat for twenty minutes unable to move. What she most fears is that she will never be free of the intersection. What she most hopes, though she says it quietly, is that someone might help her believe it is finally over.
